body.text: Standards for artificial intelligence (AI) across technical, managerial, and ethical domains are taking shape—and much of the world has little say in them. The Global North continues to exert disproportionate influence across international standards bodies, including the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). While the Global South’s formal participation has shown an uptick, it has yet to translate into commensurate influence over agenda-setting, editorial leadership, and standards drafting. ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 illustrates this gap: Southern countries, such as India and Brazil, remain a minority among its 58 voting members, despite representing the majority of the world’s population. Its secretariat is based in the United States and its five core working groups are predominantly led from the North, with China as the sole exception. The South’s participation in global AI standardisation, therefore, remains largely marginal or symbolic at best—stemming in part from resource constraints and structural disadvantages, with the United States and China alone accounting for around two-thirds of frontier technology patents.

If the Global South remains sidelined in global AI standardisation, whether by circumstance or choice, it risks undermining its digital sovereignty, economic competitiveness, and developmental priorities. This article argues that this trajectory is neither inevitable nor irreversible, explaining how the South can move beyond passively adopting standards shaped predominantly by the Global North to become a co-architect of the emerging global AI governance landscape.

Standards define requirements for products, services, and processes, enabling quality, interoperability, trust, and efficiency across industries. However, standards are not as straightforward as they may appear—for three reasons:

First—standards embed normative and ideological values: Standards are neither neutral nor apolitical. They often reflect the negotiated ethical, social, and cultural values, as well as the interests and priorities, of their creators—whether technical experts, corporations, or nation-states. For instance, Huawei’s “New IP” proposal to the ITU-T’s Telecommunication Standardisation Advisory Group in 2019 was criticised for promoting a more centralised Internet protocol architecture and viewed as reflecting China’s techno-authoritarian approach to digital governance. At times, standards organisations can themselves embody specific values—for instance, the IETF remains grounded in its commitment to an open Internet.

Second—standards serve as strategic levers of commercial and geopolitical competition: Corporations embed their patented technologies into standards to secure licensing revenues and competitive advantages. Crucially, these standards also confer strategic benefits and leverage on their home countries. Qualcomm’s standard essential patents (SEPs) in 5G standards, for instance, have created significant commercial value for the company while reinforcing US influence over global telecommunications infrastructure and safeguarding national security.

Third—standards lock in the trajectories of technological development: Once adopted, standards could be difficult to reverse or adapt and may lock in specific technical choices, creating path dependencies for the design and development of future products and services. The persistence of the QWERTY keyboard layout illustrates this dynamic. Even as alternatives such as Dvorak have shown potential to improve typing efficiency, QWERTY’s widespread adoption across hardware, software, institutional training, and user habits has created an ecosystem of complementary technologies and practices that makes switching costly and difficult.

If the Global South remains marginalised in global AI standardisation, whether by circumstance or choice, the playing field for AI will tilt toward the values, interests, and priorities of the Global North, reinforcing existing structural asymmetries in global technological competition and governance. This could ultimately mean the South forfeiting sovereign choices, economic competitiveness, and developmental gains in an AI-enabled world.

Global South firms may be forced to retrofit products to comply with standards they had little or no role in shaping, facing additional compliance costs and delays in accessing global markets. Where such standards embed SEPs, licensing dependencies could raise the costs of AI diffusion and weaken innovation ecosystems across the region. Standards that neglect Southern regulatory contexts may force firms to navigate dual compliance—one under those standards and the other under domestic regulations—potentially increasing their compliance costs and discouraging their global expansion. Where standards overlook Southern infrastructure constraints, they may prove impractical to implement—limiting the region’s ability to access and benefit from AI on inclusive terms. Comparable dynamics have persisted for decades in Voluntary Sustainability Standards, which have constrained global market participation for agricultural producers in developing countries by failing to account for their local socio-economic realities.

Even as the Global North far surpasses the Global South in frontier AI R&D and advanced chip manufacturing, with obvious exceptions such as China and Singapore—Southern countries nevertheless occupy a significant position in the global AI value chain.

Global South countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Africa, Chile, and Argentina—collectively form the mineral backbone of the global AI computing infrastructure. India contributes nearly 20 percent of global semiconductor design talent and is steadily expanding its production capabilities, alongside Malaysia, Vietnam, and Brazil. Simultaneously, innovation labs in India are developing novel computing solutions to make AI deployment more affordable.

India, the Philippines and several African countries have become global hubs for cost-effective data labelling and annotation services for AI training, while India, Brazil, and South Africa have emerged as leading centres for adapting frontier AI innovations into impactful real-world solutions through their vibrant IT industries, developer communities, and startup ecosystems. At the same time, recognising the limitations of imported models, efforts are also underway to cultivate homegrown AI champions—such as Sarvam AI in India and Lelapa AI in South Africa—to develop AI tailored to local languages and contexts.

Countries such as India and Brazil—with large, diverse, and rapidly digitising populations—are not only major markets and strategic testbeds for frontier AI models, but also vast repositories of private data critical to developing capable, contextually relevant AI systems, particularly as public data becomes increasingly exhausted and less valuable for AI development. To capitalise on this strategic advantage, India has pioneered DEPA Training and Private Inferencing—secure, interoperable, and rights-respecting standards for private data sharing.
These assets and capabilities essentially afford Global South countries substantial leverage to embed their values, interests, and priorities in global AI standards.

Global South countries must elevate participation in international AI standards bodies to an imminent policy priority. Participation must extend beyond symbolic representation to substantive contributions throughout the standards development process, from agenda-setting and drafting to consensus-building. This will require a coordinated strategy across three key action areas:

First—empowering representation on international standards committees: Global South countries should implement targeted support measures to enable sustained meaningful participation by domestic developers, researchers, and government personnel in global AI standardisation. These could include stakeholder-specific standards literacy campaigns and technical training programs, participation subsidies for eligible researchers and innovators across public and private institutions, and public research funding structured to incentivise contributions to global AI standardisation.

Second—supporting the cultivation of homegrown capabilities: Global South countries should support and incentivise AI foresight and safety initiatives to assess the system-level impacts of AI innovations deployed across their regions. This would enable Southern countries to shift from reactive regulation towards resilient governance, while building local expertise, benchmarks, and tools for context-appropriate oversight—ultimately positioning them to make substantive contributions to global AI standardisation. Support measures could include sustained public funding for AI foresight and safety research, regulatory sandboxes for evaluating novel AI systems and safeguards, and targeted grants to address critical safety bottlenecks—as demonstrated by the IndiaAI Mission.

Third—forging strategic cross-border partnerships: Capitalising on their position in the global AI value chain, Global South countries should pursue strategic partnerships with AI-leading powers, while simultaneously deepening South–South cooperation to shape bilateral and regional AI agendas and enhance their leverage to formidably influence global AI standardisation. These cross-border partnerships may emerge through state-led diplomatic initiatives—such as the UK–India Technology Security Initiative and the US–Kenya Cooperation Agreement on AI and Digital Upskilling—or privately coordinated collaborative platforms such as the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI.

Standards have long been among the most powerful tools used by governments, corporations, and trading blocs to shape—and benefit from—technological transformations. As AI transforms economies and societies worldwide, the Global South countries must make meaningful participation in global AI standardisation an imminent policy priority to safeguard their digital sovereignty, secure their economic interests, and ensure that AI works for their people. This demands a bold recalibration of the developmental agenda, targeted investments in domestic capabilities, and the pursuit of strategic cross-border partnerships.
